extracted.intended_audience: practitioners representing trademark applicants before the USPTO (trademark attorneys and supervising counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and obligations governing electronic signature practices, supervision of non‑practitioner assistants, candor to the USPTO, communications with clients, remedial measures, and discipline for trademark practitioners before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO electronic-trademark signature requirement (37 C.F.R. § 2.193)
rubrics_metrics.description: The person named as the signatory on an electronic trademark document filed with the Office must personally enter his or her electronic signature on the document (i.e., personally enter the combination of letters, numbers, spaces and/or punctuation marks adopted as a signature, placed between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission). See 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a)(2), (c), and (e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP guidance restates: "All documents must be personally signed... The person(s) identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory. ... typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature by that person." See TMEP § 611.01(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on others signing or typing another's electronic signature
rubrics_metrics.description: Typing or otherwise entering another person's electronic signature is not a valid signature; signing the name of another person (on paper or electronically) does not serve as that person's signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit TMEP example: "Just as signing the name of another person on paper does not serve as the signature of the person whose name is written, typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature by that person." Practitioners must ensure the named signatory personally enters the signature elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation permitted but requires adequate supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners may delegate tasks to non-practitioner paraprofessionals and other non-practitioner assistants, but where tasks are delegated the practitioner must adequately supervise those non-practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate supervision includes giving appropriate instruction and monitoring non-practitioners' activities. A practitioner may be disciplined for failing to take reasonable steps to supervise paraprofessionals and other non-practitioner assistants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner's responsibility over non-practitioners (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner has responsibility over non-practitioners assisting the practitioner and must take reasonable steps to ensure compliance with USPTO rules where non-practitioners are involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure examples cited: (i) allowing filings where someone other than the named signatory electronically signed; (ii) not taking reasonable steps to learn whether non-practitioner assistants obtaining signatures were impermissibly signing (e.g., not monitoring signature process); (iii) not knowing non-practitioners were signing; and/or (iv) after learning of the practice, not promptly notifying clients about impermissibly signed filings or the potential adverse consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence and promptness in client representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to signature issues: diligence includes ensuring filings are properly signed, investigating potential signature irregularities, promptly notifying clients and the USPTO, and taking remedial actions when problems are identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate with clients (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.104(a) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: After learning of signature problems or other issues, a practitioner must promptly inform clients and reasonably explain the actual or potential adverse consequences to enable informed decisions about their representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practitioner must not delay informing clients or limit responses by asserting confidentiality without independently assessing obligations. Prompt and reasonable consultation about adverse consequences is required so clients can make informed decisions about their trademark interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward the USPTO; correction of false statements (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1), (a)(3), (b), (d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal (including the USPTO) or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made, and must take reasonable remedial measures if material evidence or statements are discovered to be false. Practitioners must disclose fraudulent conduct relating to examination of trademark applications and take reasonable remedial measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance is required even if disclosure may involve information otherwise protected by 37 C.F.R. § 11.106. Examples of remedial measures include informing the USPTO that the named signatory did not sign a document and taking steps to correct the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation and conduct prejudicial to the USPTO registration process (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) and (d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing trademark documents (including declarations) not signed by the named signatory constitutes an impliedly false representation that the named signatory actually signed the document, and such conduct can be misrepresentation or conduct prejudicial to the USPTO trademark registration process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such filings are impermissibly signed, the integrity of the federal trademark registration process is adversely affected and a resulting registration may be invalid. Practitioners are expected not to file, or allow to be filed, declarations not signed by the named signatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to take reasonable remedial measures regarding improperly signed declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner becomes aware that declarations or other filings were not properly signed, the practitioner must promptly take reasonable remedial steps to correct the impliedly false statement of material fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable remedial measures include informing the USPTO that the named signatory did not sign the document and submitting corrected signature pages (e.g., Voluntary/Preliminary Amendments). Relying solely on firm representations without independent action is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to disclose fraudulent conduct and correct material misrepresentations (general guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an obligation to disclose to the USPTO if a person is engaging in or has engaged in fraudulent conduct related to examination, and to take reasonable remedial measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The duty to disclose and remediate is emphasized even if disclosure might otherwise seem to conflict with confidentiality or firm advice; the practitioner must independently assess and comply with bar/USPTO rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning on declarations and potential criminal exposure (statement in filings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark filings' declarations often carry a warning that willful false statements are punishable by fine or imprisonment under 18 U.S.C. § 1001 and may jeopardize the validity of the application or registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must appreciate the serious legal implications of declarations signed by unauthorized signatories; these warnings underline the need for accurate signature practices and remedial action when violations occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with OED investigations and proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent agreed to cooperate with all present and future Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) investigations and proceedings pertaining to the firm and attorneys involved, providing evidence or testimony remotely if unable to appear in person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation includes providing testimony or documentary evidence as requested and assisting OED inquiries to the extent possible given jurisdictional constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary sanctions and enforcement process (public reprimand, probation, suspension procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions available and applied include public reprimand and a probationary period; failure to comply during probation can lead to an Order to Show Cause and potential suspension for up to twelve months, with a 15-day response period and further referral to the USPTO Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: OED Director may issue Order to Show Cause, deliver records and argument to USPTO Director, and request immediate suspension. The Final Order also allows OED to seek discrete discipline for misconduct that formed the basis of an Order to Show Cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of disciplinary records and notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Final Orders and disciplinary decisions are to be electronically published in the OED FOIA Reading Room and a notice of public reprimand and probation is to be published in the Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication provides public notice of disciplinary actions and summarizes findings, applicable rules violated, and imposed sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical expectation: practitioners must ensure integrity of filings relied on by USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark filings bearing declarations (e.g., TEAS Plus application, Statement of Use, Combined Declarations under Sections 8 and 15) are relied upon by the USPTO when examining, registering, and renewing marks; practitioners are reasonably expected not to file or allow to be filed declarations not signed by the named signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the USPTO relies on such declarations, practitioners must ensure accuracy of signatory representation and take corrective action when inaccuracies are discovered to protect clients' intellectual property rights and the integrity of the registration process.
